definition: Cultivate means to develop or improve something, such as a skill, habit, or piece of land, through patient, sustained effort.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word cultivate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know cultivate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Over four seasons the young pitcher cultivated a changeup that no batter in the league could read.
Tend is gentler and weaker — tending keeps something alive as it is; cultivating pushes it to grow and improve through sustained effort.
Perfect is stronger than cultivate: to perfect a skill is to finish its development completely, while cultivating is the long middle stretch of growth.

Nurture means to feed, protect, and comfort a living creature as it grows - the hands-on care of raising something young. Cultivate applies that patient tending to things that grow without being alive in the same way: a skill, a habit, a friendship, a field. You nurture the young; you cultivate what you are building.

Foster means to encourage something to develop, usually indirectly, by supplying the right conditions - a teacher fosters curiosity, a city fosters new businesses. Cultivate is direct and sustained: you work on the thing itself, over time, to make it grow. Fostering sets the stage for growth; cultivating is the season-after-season tending.

When Ivy moved to the city, she knew exactly two people.
Instead of waiting for friendships to happen, she worked at them.

She hosted a monthly soup night even when only one guest came, remembered birthdays, and followed up on every 'we should get coffee sometime.' She joined the neighborhood cleanup crew and kept showing up through the cold months.
Five years later, her kitchen table needed both leaves for soup night — a circle of friends she had deliberately cultivated.
Ivy's friendships grow because she tends them with sustained, deliberate effort over years — hosting, remembering, following up — which is what it means to cultivate something.
neutral; literal (farming) and figurative (skills, relationships)

Cultivate started in the fields — tilling soil so crops improve — and English kept that growth logic when the word went figurative: you cultivate a skill, a habit, a reputation, or a friendship by tending it deliberately over time.
If there is no sustained effort aimed at growth, cultivate is the wrong verb.

Nobody is born able to read a courtroom, Judge Okonkwo liked to say; the skill has to be grown on purpose.
As a young clerk she set out to cultivate it the way her grandfather had worked his tea terraces — patiently, directly, season after season.
She sat in on hearings during lunch, kept a notebook of jurors' faces, and rehearsed her questions against a mirror for ten minutes every night.
None of it paid off quickly.
For three years the notebook showed more errors than insights.
By the time she argued her first major case, colleagues called her courtroom sense a gift.
She knew it for what it was: a crop, raised by hand over a decade.
